stories.original:
**Open banking fraud rates sit below wider UK payment benchmarks**

*Open Banking Limited's first payments and fraud monitor shows open banking fraud at roughly one in 6,000 transactions, below industry-wide rates, as payment volumes continue to climb.*

The monitor, published by Open Banking Limited, provides the first dedicated dataset on fraud within open banking payment flows. The one-in-6,000 rate compares favourably to broader UK payment fraud benchmarks, though OBL acknowledged a slight uptick in 2026 as volumes have scaled. The data covers payments initiated through open banking APIs and is intended to be published regularly.

The timing matters. Open banking payments are being adopted in higher-risk contexts such as gambling affordability checks and government services, where fraud performance data has been conspicuously absent. A dedicated monitor gives the ecosystem something concrete to point to when regulators and merchants ask whether the channel is safe enough for mainstream use.

The figures also feed into the commercial case for pay-by-bank at checkout. Card scheme fraud rates are well-documented; open banking has lacked an equivalent public benchmark. Whether one-in-6,000 holds as volumes scale further, particularly into e-commerce, is the question that matters next.

*Sources: [Open Banking Maintains Lower Fraud Rates Than the Wider Payments Industry, New Monitor Shows](https://financialit.net/news/open-banking/open-banking-maintains-lower-fraud-rates-wider-payments-industry-new-monitor-shows) — Financial IT | [Open banking fraud rates remain below wider UK payments industry benchmarks](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110354/open-banking-fraud-rates-remain-below-wider-uk-payments-industry-benchmarks) — Finextra | [Open Banking Fraud Rates Beat Industry Benchmarks Despite Rising Scam Sophistication](https://ffnews.com/news/open-banking-fraud-rates-beat-industry-benchmarks-despite-rising-scam-sophistication) — FF News*

stories.original:
**Gambling Commission confirms financial risk assessments using open banking**

*The UK Gambling Commission has confirmed it will require operators to conduct financial risk assessments on customers, with open banking as one of the approved methods for data collection.*

The Commission's announcement ends a prolonged period of industry uncertainty about how affordability checks will work in practice. Operators will be able to use open banking data or request documents directly from customers to assess financial risk. The largest operators will be required to implement the checks first, with a phased rollout to follow.

The gambling industry has resisted financial checks for years, arguing they drive customers to unregulated offshore sites. Open banking has been positioned as a less intrusive alternative to document-based checks, since it can provide a real-time view of a customer's financial position without requiring manual evidence gathering. The Commission's decision to include it as an approved method validates that argument, at least in principle.

How operators implement these checks will determine whether open banking's role in gambling regulation is substantive or cosmetic. The consent experience, data scope and frequency of checks all remain to be tested at scale.

*Sources: [Gambling Commission confirms introduction of financial risk assessments](https://www.gamingintelligence.com/legal/233006-uk-gambling-commission-confirms-introduction-of-financial-risk-assessments/) — Gaming Intelligence*

**Yapily extends open banking account verification to Google Cloud across Europe**

*Yapily has made open banking-based bank account verification available to Google Cloud business customers in eleven European markets, embedding financial data checks into cloud infrastructure.*

The integration allows Google Cloud customers to verify bank account ownership through open banking APIs without building direct connections to banks themselves. Yapily provides the connectivity layer across eleven markets, covering the major eurozone economies and the UK.

The deal is less about Yapily's product than about the distribution channel. Embedding open banking verification into a hyperscaler's marketplace shifts the buyer from fintech teams to broader enterprise procurement. For account verification specifically, this positions open banking as a cloud-native utility rather than a specialist financial service.

It also signals how open banking infrastructure providers are competing on distribution rather than connectivity alone. API coverage across European banks is increasingly commoditised; the differentiator is where and how easily those APIs can be consumed.

*Sources: [Yapily expands bank account verification for Google Cloud](https://thepaypers.com/fintech/news/yapily-brings-bank-account-verification-to-google-cloud-in-europe) — The Paypers*

**Paytm secures Luxembourg licence to build European payments operation**

*India's Paytm has obtained a payment institution licence from Luxembourg's CSSF, giving it a regulatory base to offer payment services across the European Economic Area.*

Paytm Europe Payments SA will use the Luxembourg licence to passport payment services into other EU member states. The move marks Paytm's formal entry into European regulated payments, building on its domestic position as India's largest digital payments platform.

The licence is notable for what it represents about the direction of Indian fintech expansion. Paytm joins a growing list of non-European payment firms, such as Airwallex and PhotonPay, using EEA licences to access the single market. Luxembourg continues to be the preferred jurisdiction for these entries, given its regulatory familiarity with complex cross-border structures.

Whether Paytm builds a meaningful European business or simply uses the licence to serve Indian diaspora and cross-border corridors remains to be seen. The licence itself is the enabling step, not the strategy.

*Sources: [Paytm secures Luxembourg licence to expand European payments](https://thepaypers.com/payments/news/paytm-secures-luxembourg-licence-to-expand-european-payments) — The Paypers*

**JPMorgan and Bank of America explore acquiring Fiserv's debit network**

*Two of the largest US banks are in discussions to buy Fiserv's STAR debit network, a move that could reshape card network ownership and competition in the US.*

The Wall Street Journal reported that Fiserv has held discussions with JPMorgan and Bank of America, among others, about a potential sale of its debit payments network. STAR is one of the largest PIN debit networks in the US, routing transactions for thousands of financial institutions.

Bank ownership of a major debit network would represent a structural shift in US payments. The Durbin amendment requires merchants to have access to at least two unaffiliated debit networks on every card, making STAR's routing volume commercially significant. If a bank-led consortium acquired it, the competitive dynamics between bank-owned and independent networks would change materially.

For European observers, the deal is worth watching because it echoes the sovereignty and ownership debates playing out around EPI and domestic scheme alternatives to Visa and Mastercard. The question of who owns payment rails, and what incentives that creates, is not unique to Europe.

*Sources: [JPMorgan and BofA explore acquisition of Fiserv debit network - WSJ](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48052/jpmorgan-and-bofa-explore-acquisition-of-fiserv-debit-network---wsj) — Finextra*
